topics.title: Spectral Broadening and Sample Volume
topics.frontClue: A clean black window under the peak means orderly flow; when it fills in, either the vessel or your settings are to blame.
topics.corePiece: The spectral display plots time on the horizontal axis, Doppler shift or velocity on the vertical axis, and signal amplitude, the number of reflectors, as brightness. Laminar flow in a normal artery produces a narrow band of velocities with a clear spectral window beneath the systolic peak. Spectral broadening is the filling in of that window as the range of velocities widens. True causes include disturbed or turbulent flow just beyond a stenosis, at branches and bifurcations, and in tortuous segments. Instrument causes include a sample volume that is too large or near the wall, excessive Doppler gain, an angle near 90 degrees, and small vessels in which the gate covers the whole lumen. For arterial velocity, use a small gate of about 1.5 to 2 mm centered in the lumen or in the jet; a gate spanning the lumen is used for volume flow and venous work. Poststenotic turbulence shows simultaneous forward and reverse components and a chaotic, bruit-like spectrum. Spectral mirror image, a copy of the signal across the baseline, results from high gain or near-perpendicular angles.
topics.whyLock: Spectral broadening signals flow disturbance, but it is only meaningful once instrument causes are excluded. Traps include calling the normal flow separation in a carotid bulb disease, diagnosing stenosis from broadening without a velocity increase, and mistaking mirror artifact for bidirectional flow. Small vessels such as tibial or vertebral arteries can show broadening simply because the gate fills the lumen. Poststenotic turbulence is valuable because it confirms that an elevated velocity comes from a real lesion.

topics.title: Color, Power Doppler and Artifacts
topics.frontClue: Red does not mean artery; it means toward the probe, and only if your settings are honest.
topics.corePiece: Color Doppler uses autocorrelation to estimate mean velocity and direction at many points, coding color by direction relative to the transducer, not by artery versus vein. The color bar shows the scale (Nyquist limit) and which color means flow toward the probe. Frame rate falls as box width, line density, depth and ensemble (packet) size increase, so keep the box small. The wall filter removes low-frequency clutter from wall motion; set too high, it erases slow flow. Power (amplitude or energy) Doppler displays the strength of the Doppler signal rather than velocity, usually without direction, is nearly angle independent, does not alias and is more sensitive to slow flow, at the cost of more flash artifact. Common artifacts include color bleed over walls and thrombus from excessive gain, flash from tissue or patient motion, mirror image of a vessel beneath a strong reflector such as the subclavian artery over the pleura, twinkling behind calcification, and absent color at 90 degrees.
topics.whyLock: Color settings decide whether you find slow flow, a residual lumen or a thrombus, so technique questions are common. Traps include equating red with arterial flow, overgaining so bleed covers nonocclusive thrombus or plaque, raising the wall filter or scale until a string sign vanishes, and calling a subclavian mirror image a duplicate artery. Before reporting occlusion, lower the scale and wall filter, raise color gain to just below noise, try power Doppler, and confirm with spectral Doppler.

topics.title: Resistive Index, Pulsatility Index, Acceleration Time and Safety
topics.frontClue: Ratios do not care about angle, and the slow climb to a peak tells you trouble lies upstream.
topics.corePiece: Resistive index (RI, Pourcelot) equals (PSV minus EDV) divided by PSV; values near 1 indicate high resistance and lower values low resistance. Normal intrarenal RI is about 0.6 to 0.7, and values above about 0.7 to 0.8 are considered elevated. Pulsatility index (PI, Gosling) equals (PSV minus EDV) divided by the time-averaged mean velocity; it reflects waveform shape and can exceed 1. Normal resting leg arteries often have a PI above 5 to 6, transcranial PI is about 0.6 to 1.1, and a PI that falls from proximal to distal suggests disease in between. Acceleration time runs from the start of systole to the first systolic peak; values above about 0.07 s in intrarenal or tibial arteries indicate a tardus parvus pattern from proximal obstruction. For safety, the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable) governs output and dwell time. The thermal index (TIS soft tissue, TIB bone, TIC cranial bone) estimates heating, and the mechanical index estimates cavitation risk, rising with peak rarefactional pressure and falling with higher frequency.
topics.whyLock: Because indices are ratios, they are independent of angle, which makes them useful for intrarenal and transcranial work where angle correction is unreliable. Traps include mixing up RI and PI formulas (PI divides by mean velocity), assuming a high RI always means disease (it rises with age, bradycardia and extrinsic compression), and forgetting that acceleration time lengthens distal to a stenosis. For safety items, raise receiver gain before raising output power, minimize dwell time, and remember that pulsed Doppler carries the greatest thermal risk.

topics.title: Key Velocity and Pressure Criteria
topics.frontClue: One page of numbers that answers half the exam, as long as you do not swap them between vessels.
topics.corePiece: Carotid, SRU consensus, with ICA PSV as the primary parameter: normal ICA PSV under 125 cm/s with no plaque; under 50 percent, PSV under 125 cm/s with plaque and ICA/CCA ratio under 2; 50 to 69 percent, PSV 125 to 230 cm/s, ratio 2 to 4, EDV 40 to 100 cm/s; 70 percent or more, PSV over 230 cm/s, ratio over 4, EDV over 100 cm/s; near occlusion shows a string sign. Leg arteries: PSV ratio 2 or more means 50 percent or greater stenosis. ABI: over 1.4 noncompressible; 1.0 to 1.4 normal; 0.91 to 0.99 borderline; 0.9 or less PAD, and 0.4 or less severe. TBI under 0.7 is abnormal. Renal: PSV over 180 to 200 cm/s with RAR over 3.5. Mesenteric, fasting: SMA 275 cm/s or more, celiac 200 cm/s or more. Reflux: over 0.5 s superficial, deep femoral, calf and perforator veins; over 1 s common femoral, femoral and popliteal. AAA: 3 cm or more. Vein graft at high risk: PSV over 300 cm/s with a ratio over 3.5, or mid-graft PSV under 45 cm/s.
topics.whyLock: The registry rewards fast recall of thresholds, and many distractors are real numbers borrowed from a neighboring criterion. Traps include swapping carotid 125 and 230 cm/s cutoffs with renal or mesenteric values, applying the 0.5 s superficial reflux rule to the femoral vein, calling an ABI over 1.4 normal, and using a ratio when the reference segment is itself abnormal. Some criteria, such as renal and mesenteric thresholds, vary by lab, so registry answers usually follow the most widely cited consensus.

topics.title: Critical Findings and Follow-Up Intervals
topics.frontClue: Some results cannot wait in the report queue; the rest come back on a schedule set by how close they are to treatment.
topics.corePiece: Critical findings need direct, documented communication to a responsible provider, not just a written report: record who was told, when and how. Typical vascular critical results include acute proximal DVT (popliteal or above), superficial thrombus within about 3 cm of the SFJ or SPJ, free-floating thrombus, acute arterial occlusion or limb ischemia, a symptomatic, rapidly enlarging or ruptured aortic aneurysm, a new carotid occlusion or high-grade stenosis in a symptomatic patient, carotid dissection, a failing bypass graft (PSV over 300 cm/s with a ratio over 3.5, or mid-graft PSV under 45 cm/s), a postcatheterization pseudoaneurysm, a type I or III endoleak, and suspected acute mesenteric ischemia. Common follow-up intervals: a negative limited DVT exam with ongoing suspicion is repeated in 5 to 7 days; isolated calf DVT under surveillance in 1 to 2 weeks; AAA 3.0 to 3.9 cm about every 3 years, 4.0 to 4.9 cm yearly, and 5.0 to 5.4 cm every 6 months; after EVAR at about 1 and 12 months, then yearly; vein grafts at about 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, then yearly.
topics.whyLock: Recognizing and communicating a critical result is a professional duty and a frequent scenario question. Traps include leaving a voicemail or relying on the electronic report alone, delaying the call because the study was technically limited, and treating an incidental AAA as unimportant. Intervals vary by society and lab, so registry answers usually follow major guidelines; the logic is that the closer a finding is to an intervention threshold, the shorter the interval. Always document the communication in the report.
